confirmed.title: All 401 responses are collapsed into SessionExpiredError, destroying real business-logic 401s
confirmed.detail: apiFetch treats every non-skipAuth 401 as a session-refresh event: on 401 it calls refreshSession(), retries once, and if the retry still returns 401 it throws `new SessionExpiredError({message:'Session expired', status:401})` (client.ts:210-215, :219-222) — discarding the server's real message/code entirely. The backend does not reserve 401 for token expiry only: `deleteMyAccount` in server/src/controllers/user.controller.ts explicitly does `throw ApiError.unauthorized('Password is incorrect')` for a wrong delete-account password, using the exact same `code:'UNAUTHORIZED'` as auth.middleware.ts's token-expired/invalid-token 401s (server/src/utils/ApiError.ts:74-76, server/src/middlewares/auth.middleware.ts:46-51). So: user has a valid session but types the wrong account-deletion password → first 401 → client auto-refreshes the (perfectly valid) access token → retries the DELETE with the same wrong password → still 401 → client throws SessionExpiredError, permanently losing the 'Password is incorrect' message/code. It happens to still display the right copy in use-trust.ts today only because `error.status===401` matches for both real and fake causes (see next finding for why that's itself broken), but any endpoint returning a non-refreshable 401 for a reason other than token expiry gets silently mis-handled by this blanket refresh-and-retry path, and 2 wasted network calls (refresh + retry) are burned on every such request.
confirmed.fix: Distinguish token-expiry 401s from business-logic 401s before triggering the refresh/retry dance — e.g. only auto-refresh when the response carries a specific auth-token error code (add one server-side, e.g. TOKEN_EXPIRED/INVALID_TOKEN vs UNAUTHORIZED for domain checks), or only apply the refresh-and-retry path to a whitelisted set of routes, and otherwise surface the original ApiError (message/code) to the caller unchanged.
confirmed.verifyReason:
The core technical claim is fully verified against the actual code. mobile/src/services/api/client.ts:198-223 confirms: any non-skipAuth 401 triggers refreshSession() + one retry, and if the retry still returns 401, the client throws `new SessionExpiredError({message:'Session expired', status:401})` unconditionally — discarding the server's real body/message/code (client.ts:210-215, 219-222). SessionExpiredError extends ApiError (services/api/errors.ts), so it is indistinguishable from a real ApiError with status 401 to any `instanceof ApiError && status===401` check downstream.

The server-side counterexample is real and reachable: server/src/controllers/user.controller.ts:225 does `throw ApiError.unauthorized('Password is incorrect')` for a wrong delete-account password, using ApiError.unauthorized (server/src/utils/ApiError.ts:74-76), which always sets `code:'UNAUTHORIZED'` — the exact same status/code auth.middleware.ts uses for expired/invalid tokens (auth.middleware.ts:46-51). mobile/src/services/api/trust.ts:30-34 confirms deleteMyAccount's DELETE /v1/users/me call goes through apiFetch with default skipAuth=false, so the full refresh-and-retry-and-collapse path applies. I surveyed other controllers using ApiError.unauthorized() (task, message, chat, groups, follow, accountability-contract, voice-call, etc.) and all other instances found are `if (!userId) throw ApiError.unauthorized()` auth-middleware-adjacent guards, not genuine domain 401s — deleteMyAccount is the one clean, demonstrated business-logic 401 in the codebase today, which is enough to prove the pattern is real, not hypothetical.

However, the finding overstates present-day user impact, and even says so itself: mobile/src/hooks/use-trust.ts:122-123 does `if (error instanceof ApiError && error.status === 401) setErrorMessage('Password is incorrect')`, so today's single real-world trigger of this bug still renders the correct copy by coincidence (status-code match), at the cost of two wasted network round-trips (refresh + retry) and added latency before the (correct) error surfaces. There is no data loss, no security bypass, and no currently-broken/incorrect message shown to any user — the failure mode described is a real and verified architectural landmine for any *future* or currently-unaudited business-logic 401, not a presently manifesting critical defect. That gap between 'proven code smell/latent bug' and 'critical, user-visible breakage today' means the severity should be downgraded from critical to medium. The proposed fix (distinguish token-expiry error codes from domain UNAUTHORIZED before triggering refresh/retry, or scope the refresh dance to a whitelist of endpoints) is correct, minimal, and directly addresses the root cause.

confirmed.title: SessionExpiredError extends ApiError, so delete-account error handling cannot tell 'wrong password' from 'your session actually died'
confirmed.detail: `SessionExpiredError extends ApiError` (mobile/src/services/api/errors.ts:23), and both are thrown with `status:401`. useDeleteAccount's catch does `if (error instanceof ApiError && error.status === 401) setErrorMessage('Password is incorrect')` — this branch fires identically whether the underlying cause was actually a wrong password OR a genuinely expired/rotated session (e.g. the multi-device refresh-token-mismatch case documented in session.ts:116-118, or a fully expired refresh token). In the real-session-expired case the user is told 'Password is incorrect' (false), retries with the same correct password, gets the same message again, and is never prompted to re-authenticate — because nothing here (or anywhere else, see next finding) forces a sign-out/redirect to login on SessionExpiredError from this mutation.
confirmed.fix: Check `error instanceof SessionExpiredError` first (route to a re-auth prompt / forced sign-out) and only fall through to the generic ApiError 401 branch for actual delete-account domain errors — which requires client.ts to stop erasing the distinguishing signal (see previous finding).
confirmed.verifyReason:
Code reads exactly as claimed. errors.ts:23 `export class SessionExpiredError extends ApiError {}` means every SessionExpiredError instance also satisfies `instanceof ApiError`, and client.ts always constructs SessionExpiredError with a hardcoded `status: 401` (lines 211-222). use-trust.ts:122's check `error instanceof ApiError && error.status === 401` therefore matches both a genuine wrong-password 401 from the server (user.controller.ts:225 `ApiError.unauthorized('Password is incorrect')`) and a SessionExpiredError thrown when refresh fails or the retried request still 401s — there is no branch anywhere that special-cases SessionExpiredError for this mutation (unlike session-provider.tsx's `/auth/me` calls, which do check `instanceof SessionExpiredError` and force a sign-out dispatch). The delete-account path has no equivalent, so a real session death is caught by the generic branch and mapped to the same hardcoded 'Password is incorrect' string, with no forced re-auth/sign-out.

This is also compounded by client.ts's blanket 401 handler (line 205: `if (response.status === 401 && !skipAuth)`), which intercepts every 401 on an authed endpoint — including the domain-level 'wrong password' 401 from DELETE /v1/users/me — attempts a refresh, retries once, and if that retry still 401s, discards the server's real message and throws a generic SessionExpiredError. So in practice almost every 401 this mutation can produce, including plain wrong-password, already arrives at use-trust.ts as a SessionExpiredError instance, not a bare ApiError — making the two cases even less distinguishable than the finding assumes, not less real.

One nuance worth flagging: the sole current consumer, data-controls-screen.tsx, destructures only `{ run: runDelete, running: deleting }` from useDeleteAccount and never reads/renders the hook's `error` value, so today no message (correct or false) is actually painted to the screen on failure — the user instead sees a silent no-op (button returns to idle with zero feedback), not literally the text 'Password is incorrect' as the finding's narrative states. That's a real gap in the finding's precise user-visible framing, but it does not refute the underlying code defect: the classification logic at use-trust.ts:122 is genuinely unable to distinguish the two error types, `error` is clearly meant to be surfaced (it's returned from the hook precisely for that purpose), and once wired up (or for any future/other consumer of this hook) it will show exactly the false message the finding describes. The proposed fix (check `instanceof SessionExpiredError` before falling through to the generic `ApiError && status===401` branch, and route it to a forced re-auth/sign-out) is correct and minimal, and correctly notes it depends on client.ts no longer erasing the real domain-401 signal first.

confirmed.title: SessionExpiredError from any screen besides boot()/refreshUser() never transitions the global session state — app gets stuck 'authenticated' with dead queries
confirmed.detail: `REFRESH_FAILURE` (session-machine.ts) is only ever dispatched from two call sites: the boot() background /auth/me validate (session-provider.tsx:107-114) and refreshUser() (session-provider.tsx:76-83). `refreshUser` itself is exposed on the session context but is never called anywhere in the app (verified: no screen/hook calls `useSession().refreshUser()`). Every data query — useOverview, useMissions, useLifeAreas, useFitness, useGamification, usePreferences, useOnboardingStatus, useDeleteAccount, useCiaChat — calls apiFetch directly and, per query/client.ts:9-12, TanStack Query is explicitly told not to retry on SessionExpiredError, but nothing there (or anywhere) dispatches REFRESH_FAILURE or forces sign-out when one of THESE queries throws SessionExpiredError. Result: if the refresh token is invalidated mid-session (e.g. another device signs in and rotates the single stored refresh token, per session.ts:116-118), every screen but the boot/me screen just sits on a permanently failed query with the session machine still reporting 'authenticated' — the user is never routed back to /(auth)/sign-in and local storage is never cleared, until they force-quit and relaunch the app (which re-runs boot()).
confirmed.fix: Add a global handler (e.g. a TanStack `QueryCache({onError})` in query/client.ts, or a subscription in SessionProvider) that catches SessionExpiredError from any query/mutation and dispatches REFRESH_FAILURE + clearSession() + handleAuthCleared() exactly once, so the app always falls back to the sign-in screen regardless of which query first noticed the dead session.
confirmed.verifyReason: Read all relevant files: session-provider.tsx, session-machine.ts, session.ts, query/client.ts, api/client.ts, errors.ts, plus routing (app/index.tsx, (tabs)/_layout.tsx) and representative query hooks (use-overview.ts, use-missions.ts). Confirmed line-by-line: (1) REFRESH_FAILURE is dispatched from exactly two sites — boot()'s background /auth/me validate (session-provider.tsx:107-114) and refreshUser() (line 76-83) — nothing else in the codebase dispatches it (grep confirms). (2) refreshUser is exported on the context but grep shows zero call sites anywhere in src/app or src/hooks — it is dead code from the app's perspective. (3) All data-query hooks (use-overview.ts, use-missions.ts, and by consistent pattern use-life-areas/use-fitness/use-gamification/use-preferences/use-onboarding-status/use-cia-chat) call apiFetch directly inside queryFn with no error handling; query/client.ts:9-12 confirms retry is explicitly disabled for SessionExpiredError but there is no QueryCache/MutationCache onError, and grep for 'onError|QueryCache|subscribe' across src turns up nothing related to session recovery. (4) Routing is driven purely by session-machine status: app/index.tsx and (tabs)/_layout.tsx redirect to sign-in only on 'unauthenticated'/'expired' status, not on any query error state. (5) session.ts:115-119 shows refreshSession() does call clearSession() on a detected token mismatch/expiry (the multi-device rotation scenario), but that only wipes SecureStore — it never touches the React session-machine state, so status remains 'authenticated' and the tabs layout does not redirect. The reducer even has unused REFRESH_START/REFRESH_SUCCESS transitions (only exercised in the unit test, never dispatched in the provider), corroborating that the refresh-recovery wiring is genuinely incomplete, not an intentional design the reviewer misread. No waiver or doc reference to this behavior was found in mobile/docs. The scenario is concrete and reachable (any authenticated screen's background query hits the single-refresh-token-rotation case), not out-of-scope, and the proposed fix (a global onError hook — QueryCache/MutationCache in query/client.ts, or a registered callback the SessionProvider subscribes to — that dispatches REFRESH_FAILURE + clearSession + handleAuthCleared exactly once) is architecturally correct and minimal given the existing setAuthTokenProvider/setRefreshHandler/setStaleGuard registration pattern already used between client.ts and session-provider.tsx.

confirmed.title: Recovery/stress metrics are force-nulled whenever hasWearable is false, discarding real backend-computed values
confirmed.detail: `mapPulseMetric` unconditionally returns `nullMetric('Connect a wearable')` for `key==='recovery'||key==='stress'` whenever `!hasWearable`, before even checking `metric.value`/`metric.source`. But the vendored DTO's own doc comment (dto/overview.ts:252-259) states the backend computes real recovery/stress from self-reported sleep/mood/workout/nutrition data when no wearable is connected and marks it `source:'computed'` — a legitimate, honesty-compliant real value the mobile Metric/provenance system already has a path for (`realMetric`/`pulseMetricLabels.computed`). For any user who has been logging health data without a WHOOP, the adapter throws away that real computed number and shows a misleading 'Connect a wearable' locked state instead of the actual server-provided value — the opposite of the honesty invariant (suppressing real data rather than inventing fake data), and a functional regression for wearable-less users specifically because the current recorded fixture happens to have `value:null` for a brand-new account, masking the bug in the recorded contract test.
confirmed.fix: Only fall back to `nullMetric('Connect a wearable')` when `metric.value === null` (i.e. rely on the existing null-check on the next line) — drop the separate hasWearable-based override, or if the intent is genuinely to hide computed recovery/stress without a wearable, that policy needs to be a documented product decision, not a silent adapter-level override of server-attested real data.
confirmed.verifyReason: Code at overview.ts:56-58 exactly matches the claim: mapPulseMetric unconditionally returns nullMetric('Connect a wearable') for key==='recovery'||'stress' whenever !hasWearable, before the metric.value null-check on the next line. Verified against dto/overview.ts:252-259 doc comment and server/src/services/life-pulse.service.ts:299-341, which show the backend deliberately computes real recovery/stress values from self-reported wellbeing components (source:'computed', with real trend data) precisely when no WHOOP is connected (hasWearable = whoopRecovery/whoopStress != null), and explicitly documents this as honesty-compliant behavior ('when absent we compute from app data ... and mark source: computed'). The mobile adapter discards that real computed value and forces a locked 'Connect a wearable' empty state instead — a genuine regression for wearable-less users who have real self-reported/computed data (non-null value + source:'computed'). Also confirmed the masking claim: mobile/src/services/adapters/overview.test.ts uses a fixture that is explicitly the fresh-account state (hasWearable:false AND value:null), so the override path is never exercised against a non-null computed value in the recorded contract test, hiding the bug. The proposed fix (drop the hasWearable-based override and rely on the existing metric.value===null check, or else make hiding computed values an explicit documented product decision) is correct and minimal — it leaves the legitimate null-value honesty path on the next line untouched, and provenance.ts's realMetric/pulseMetricLabels.computed already supports rendering a 'computed' labeled real value, so no new plumbing is needed. Not out of scope, not a misreading, not duplicating documented behavior — the DTO doc comment documents the opposite of what the adapter currently does.

confirmed.title: Honesty invariant violation: null completion rate rendered as a fake "0"
confirmed.detail: `data.activePlan.completionRate` is a `Metric<number>` produced by `fromNullable()` (services/adapters/fitness.ts) specifically so a missing value stays `null` with provenance `{kind:'null', label:'Not enough data yet'}`. The screen then does `value={data.activePlan.completionRate.value ?? 0}` when feeding `StatBar`. `StatBar` (components/balencia/charts.tsx:23-36) unconditionally renders `Math.round(value)` as a visible numeric label plus a filled progress track. When completion rate is null, the user sees a literal "0" and an empty-but-present bar directly under a ProvenanceChip that says "Not enough data yet" — i.e. an invented number sits right next to the honest null indicator, contradicting it.
confirmed.fix: Guard the render: only mount `<StatBar .../>` when `completionRate.value !== null`, and show a null/empty treatment (e.g. `HonestNullState` or omit the bar) when it is null — mirroring how the rest of the screen already branches on `.value === null` for other metrics.
confirmed.verifyReason: Code matches the finding exactly. mobile/src/services/adapters/fitness.ts:32 builds completionRate via fromNullable(rawActivePlan.overallCompletionRate, {source:'server', label:'from your plan'}); when the raw value is null/undefined, provenance.ts's fromNullable returns nullMetric(), i.e. {value: null, display: '—', provenance: {kind:'null', label:'Not enough data yet'}}. fitness-screen.tsx:60 renders a ProvenanceChip showing that honest 'Not enough data yet' label, then line 62-66 immediately does value={data.activePlan.completionRate.value ?? 0} into <StatBar>. charts.tsx's StatBar (lines 23-36) unconditionally computes percent from the numeric value and renders <Text>{Math.round(value)}</Text> plus a filled progress track — there is no null-branch inside StatBar itself. So when completionRate is null, the screen renders a literal '0' and a rendered (0%-filled but structurally present) bar directly beneath a chip that says data isn't available — an invented number sitting next to the honest null indicator, which is a real, verifiable, user-visible contradiction. This is exactly the pattern the codebase itself treats as a hard error elsewhere: today-screen.tsx:56-58 explicitly branches `lifePower.value === null ? <HonestNullState .../> : <actual UI/>` rather than coalescing to 0, and mobile/AGENTS.md states 'Every backend gap needs a visible readiness/provenance state' — fitness-screen.tsx's completionRate treatment breaks that established, documented convention while sibling metrics in the same file (score, recovery, weeklyMinutes) and sibling screens correctly gate on null. The proposed fix (guard StatBar's mount on `completionRate.value !== null`, render HonestNullState/omit otherwise) is correct, minimal, and consistent with the exact pattern already used elsewhere in this file and today-screen.tsx — no scope creep, not a visual-parity/BIOS-004 concern, and not duplicating already-intended behavior.

confirmed.title: Me screen has no loading/error state for gamification stats — silently renders fabricated Level 0 / 0 XP / Streak 0
confirmed.detail: `useGamification()` (hooks/use-gamification.ts) returns a TanStack Query result with `status`, exactly like `useOverview`, `useMissions`, `useLifeAreas`, and `useFitness` — all of which branch on `status === 'pending'`/`'error'` before rendering. `me-screen.tsx` instead destructures only `{ data: stats }` (line 12) and renders `MetricTile` with `stats?.level ?? 0`, `stats?.xp.toLocaleString() ?? 0`, `stats?.streak ?? 0` (lines 20-21) with no pending/error branch at all. While the query is loading, or if it errors, the user sees a confident "Level 0 / 0 XP" and "Streak 0" — indistinguishable from a real level-0 account — instead of a skeleton or error state.
confirmed.fix: Destructure `status` from `useGamification()` and add the same pending/error branches used by every other data screen in this batch (SkeletonState while pending, ErrorState with retry on error) before rendering the MetricTiles.
confirmed.verifyReason:
Verified directly against the source. me-screen.tsx line 12 does `const { data: stats } = useGamification();` — no `status`/`refetch` destructured, no pending/error branch anywhere in the component (confirmed by reading the full 67-line file). useGamification() (hooks/use-gamification.ts) is a plain useQuery wrapping toStatsView, which itself defaults every field (level ?? 1, xp ?? 0, streak ?? 0) — so `stats` is `undefined` while pending/erroring, and MetricTile at lines 20-21 falls through to its own `?? 0` defaults, rendering "Level 0 / 0 XP" and "Streak 0" indistinguishable from a genuine level-0 new user. This is a real, user-visible ambiguous-state bug, not a misread.

Sibling screens in the same batch establish the intended pattern unambiguously: today-screen.tsx (`const { data, status, refetch } = useOverview()`) and fitness-screen.tsx (`const { data, status, refetch } = useFitness()`) both explicitly branch on `status === 'pending'` → SkeletonState and `status === 'error' || !data` → ErrorState before rendering any metric, importing the same SkeletonState/ErrorState components that are already available in `@/components/balencia` (me-screen.tsx doesn't even import them). me-screen.tsx is the outlier that skips this, so it's squarely in-scope/inconsistent with the batch's own established convention, not a documented exception or out-of-scope deep-visual-parity concern.

The proposed fix (destructure `status`/`refetch`, add pending→SkeletonState and error→ErrorState branches matching today-screen/fitness-screen) is correct, minimal, and directly mirrors the existing sibling pattern with no invented abstractions.</reason>

confirmed.title: Purple mapped to the Weekly Mission tier chip — non-Cia surface color-role violation
confirmed.detail: `tierTone.weekly = 'purple'` maps the Weekly Mission tier to the purple accent on the Missions screen, which is not a Cia/AI surface. Purple (#7F24FF) is reserved 60/30/10-canon for Cia/AI indicators only. `MissionsVM['tier']` (services/adapters/missions.ts) is currently typed `'life' | 'main' | 'side'` so this key is unreachable today, but it is live source code mapping a non-AI RPG tier to the AI-only color — the moment `mapTier()` is extended to emit `'weekly'` (e.g. once the backend distinguishes cadence), purple leaks onto the Missions board with no review gate catching it.
confirmed.fix: Remove the `weekly`/`daily` purple/green entries from `tierTone` (they don't correspond to any value `MissionVM['tier']` can hold) or replace `purple` with a non-AI tone (e.g. a steel/gray mapped onto an existing non-purple chip tone) so no code path can ever paint a Mission chip purple.
confirmed.verifyReason: Verified against live code. mobile/src/features/missions/missions-screen.tsx:17-23 defines `tierTone = { life: 'orange', main: 'muted', side: 'warning', daily: 'green', weekly: 'purple' }`, and line 22 (`tierTone[mission.tier]`, used at ~line 79) is indexed by `mission.tier`. `MissionTier` in services/adapters/missions.ts:3 is `'life' | 'main' | 'side'` only, and `mapTier()` (lines 29-37) can only ever return one of those three — confirmed by grepping the whole mobile/src tree: no code anywhere assigns or tests a `'weekly'`/`'daily'` tier value. So `tierTone.weekly`/`.daily` are dead, unreachable entries today, exactly as the finding states. `BalenciaColors.purple` (constants/theme.ts:18) resolves to `#7F24FF`, which is precisely the royal-purple documented in this repo's own CLAUDE.md as reserved 60/30/10-canon for Cia/AI-indicator use only — confirming the color-role claim, not a misreading. `StatusChip`'s `ChipTone` (components/balencia/chips.tsx) does include a `'purple'` tone already used elsewhere for an AI-adjacent case (`waiver`), reinforcing that purple is meant to be AI-scoped, not a generic tier color. The failure scenario is real but latent (correctly framed as risk-of-future-leak, not present-day visible bug), which is consistent with the reported medium severity rather than high/critical. The proposed fix — delete the two unreachable `tierTone` entries (or replace `purple` with a non-AI tone) — is correct, minimal, and directly closes the gap since no other code path depends on those two keys.

confirmed.title: Purple GlassCard used for a general paywall-discipline note, not a Cia/AI surface
confirmed.detail: `<GlassCard tone="purple">` wraps the "Premium gate discipline" card (PaywallLock/exports/revoke/WhatsApp/finance/document/compliance gating language) — this content has nothing to do with Cia or AI. Every other purple usage in the batch (cia-screen.tsx, cia-onboarding-screen.tsx, today-screen.tsx's "Cia briefing") is on an explicitly Cia-labeled surface; here purple is instead used as a generic "important/gated" signal, which is exactly the 60/30/10 misuse the canon rule prohibits (purple must stay an AI-identity color, not a general-purpose accent).
confirmed.fix: Use a non-purple tone (e.g. `orange` or `warning`-styled GlassCard) for this card since it is not a Cia/AI surface.
confirmed.verifyReason: Read mobile/src/features/trust/me-screen.tsx:38 directly — `<GlassCard tone="purple">` wraps the "Premium gate discipline" card, whose content (PaywallLock/exports/revoke/WhatsApp/finance/document/compliance gating language) has no Cia/AI connection, confirming the claim as-is. Cross-checked every other `tone="purple"` GlassCard usage in the codebase: today-screen.tsx (Cia briefing/StatusChip "Cia"), cia-screen.tsx (message.role === 'cia'), cia-onboarding-screen.tsx (Cia messages/mode) — all are explicitly Cia-labeled surfaces, exactly as the finding states. The canon (COMPONENT-CATALOG.md) repeatedly ties purple to AI-derived/CIA-only usage ("ConfidenceMeter ... purple when AI-derived", "BtnCoach ... CIA-initiated actions only", CIAInsightCard/CIAChatBubble = purple-tinted for CIA), consistent with CLAUDE.md's 60/30/10 rule that royal-purple is "SIA/AI indicators only." So the misuse is a real, documented invariant violation, not a misreading. Additionally found the same anti-pattern also present at data-controls-screen.tsx:122 (`GlassCard tone="purple"` on "Gated sources", unrelated to Cia), reinforcing this is a genuine recurring pattern rather than an isolated edge case. Scope check: me-screen.tsx is an explicit pilot route in BIOS-001's scope (not deferred to BIOS-004 visual-parity work), so it is in-batch. The proposed fix (swap to a non-purple tone) is directionally correct and minimal — GlassCard's card.tsx already defines an `orange` tone that could be reused immediately; the finding's alternate suggestion of a "warning"-styled GlassCard is slightly imprecise since GlassCard (unlike StatusChip/ReadinessBadge in chips.tsx) has no `warning` tone defined today, so that part would require a small addition — but this doesn't undermine the core defect or the viable minimal fix (use existing `orange` tone). Severity of `design/medium` is reasonable for a documented brand-color-system violation on a shipped pilot screen.

confirmed.title: Purple GlassCard used for the "Gated sources" trust-center list — non-Cia surface
confirmed.detail: `<GlassCard tone="purple">` wraps the `GATED_FEATURES` list (finance, WhatsApp, documents, wearables) on the Data Controls / trust-center screen. None of this content is Cia/AI-related; it is a generic "not yet available" gating list. Same violation pattern as me-screen.tsx:38 — purple is being used as a general locked/flagged indicator rather than reserved for Cia/AI identity, contrary to the hard 60/30/10 rule.
confirmed.fix: Replace with a non-purple tone (`default` or `warning`) for this card.
confirmed.verifyReason: Read data-controls-screen.tsx:122 directly — `<GlassCard tone="purple">` wraps the 'Gated sources' card rendering GATED_FEATURES (finance, WhatsApp, documents, wearables from src/services/adapters/trust.ts), none of which are Cia/AI content; they are generic 'backend not production-ready' gating reasons. Cross-checked all 4 uses of tone="purple" in the mobile codebase: today-screen.tsx:103/106 correctly uses purple for the 'Cia briefing' card (headline text + StatusChip label='Cia'), matching the canon rule at Balencia-New-Screens/canon/COMPACT-CANON.md:7,21,74 ('CIA moments add a purple pool', 'projected/AI = dashed purple') and the top-level CLAUDE.md 60/30/10 rule (royal-purple 'SIA/AI indicators only'). me-screen.tsx:38 and data-controls-screen.tsx:122 both misuse purple for non-AI gating/flag content, exactly as the finding states — a real, consistent, documented-rule violation, not a misread. Severity/design classification is reasonable (visual-system consistency issue, not functional/security, so medium fits). One correction to the proposed fix: GlassCard's tone type (src/components/balencia/card.tsx) is only 'default' | 'orange' | 'green' | 'purple' — there is no 'warning' tone on GlassCard (that exists only on StatusChip/Chip via ChipTone). So 'default or warning' as GlassCard options is partly inaccurate; 'default' is the correct minimal fix, optionally paired with a StatusChip tone="warning" on individual gated rows (matching the ReadinessBadge 'flagged' pattern already used in me-screen.tsx) rather than a GlassCard tone="warning" that doesn't exist. This is a minor fix-detail nit, not grounds to refute the finding itself.

confirmed.title: Mission tier chips render raw tier keys ("life"/"main"/"side") instead of canon Mission terminology
confirmed.detail: `<StatusChip label={mission.tier} .../>` prints the literal adapter values `life` / `main` / `side` in lowercase with no "Mission" suffix. Canon RPG terminology names these tiers "Life Mission", "Main Mission", "Side Mission" (gold/silver/bronze) — the visible copy here doesn't match, which is a naming-canon miss (not just an unstyled-visual deferral), since it's the actual displayed word, not color/spacing.
confirmed.fix: Map `mission.tier` through a label table (e.g. `{ life: 'Life Mission', main: 'Main Mission', side: 'Side Mission' }`) before passing to `StatusChip`.
confirmed.verifyReason: Verified against mobile/src/features/missions/missions-screen.tsx:79 and the StatusChip implementation in mobile/src/components/balencia/chips.tsx: StatusChip renders `label` verbatim with zero text transformation (`<Text>{label}</Text>`), and `mission.tier` is the raw adapter enum value ('life'/'main'/'side'/'daily'/'weekly') confirmed by mobile/src/services/adapters/missions.ts (mapTier) and mobile/src/services/adapters/missions.test.ts. confirmed.title: Purple-on-purpleSoft chip text fails WCAG AA contrast (~2.8:1)

Blending purpleSoft over the actual card/screen backgrounds it's drawn on (ink900 #0A0A0F or inkBrown800 #211008) and computing WCAG relative luminance gives a contrast ratio of only ~2.8-3.0:1 for the 12px/700-weight chip label — well under the 4.5:1 AA floor required for text this size (it isn't 'large text' by the 18pt/14pt-bold thresholds). This is concretely hit at mobile/src/features/today/today-screen.tsx:106 (`<StatusChip label="Cia" tone="purple" />`), where purple is reserved for the Cia/AI indicator per canon, so it's exactly the surface that must be legible.
confirmed.fix: Lighten the purple text token for on-soft-background use (e.g. a lighter purple tint) or darken/raise the opacity of purpleSoft until the pair clears 4.5:1, and re-check every tone in chips.tsx (orange/green already sit at ~4.7-5.3:1, acceptable) the same way before shipping more purple-tone chips.

Independently recomputed WCAG relative luminance: blending purpleSoft (alpha 0.2) over screen bg ink900 (#0A0A0F) gives ~2.99:1; over inkBrown800 (#211008) gives ~2.76:1 — matching the finding's ~2.8–3.0:1 claim almost exactly. As a sanity check I recomputed orange (text #FF5E00 on orangeSoft over ink900) and got ~5.26:1, confirming the finding's claim that orange/green already clear AA while purple alone does not — same methodology, consistent result.

Confirmed the concrete usage at today-screen.tsx:106 exactly as cited (`<StatusChip label="Cia" tone="purple" />`), and went one step further: that chip is nested inside `<GlassCard tone="purple">` (card.tsx), whose own background is ALSO purpleSoft blended over ink900. confirmed.title: Cia composer has no keyboard avoidance, unlike the sign-in screen

CiaScreen (cia-screen.tsx:79-91) and CiaOnboardingScreen (cia-onboarding-screen.tsx:129-142) both place a multiline TextInput + Send button as the LAST element in the scroll content, after the messages list and any gate cards — the worst position for keyboard occlusion. The proposed fix (wrap in KeyboardAvoidingView matching sign-in-screen's pattern, or enable automaticallyAdjustKeyboardInsets on the shared ScrollView) is correct and minimal, reusing an existing in-codebase precedent. Not out of scope — this is a functional a11y/UX defect (chat composer becomes inaccessible under an open keyboard on a primary tab screen), not a visual-parity nitpick deferred to BIOS-004.

confirmed.title: Delete-account confirmation inputs have no keyboard avoidance

There is no KeyboardAvoidingView and `automaticallyAdjustKeyboardInsets` defaults to false, so the keyboard can cover these fields with no automatic scroll-into-view. This is the single most consequence-sensitive input in the batch (irreversible account deletion) and the user may not be able to see what they typed while confirming.
confirmed.fix: Wrap DataControlsScreen (or the shared BalenciaScreen) in a KeyboardAvoidingView, or explicitly scroll the delete-step-2 TextInput into view on focus.
confirmed.verifyReason: Verified directly against the code. mobile/src/features/trust/data-controls-screen.tsx:144-163 renders the delete-phrase and password TextInputs inside `<BalenciaScreen>` as the 5th of 6 GlassCards (Privacy → Export → Consent history → Gated sources → Delete account → Session control), i.e. genuinely "several cards down." On RN 0.86 (per package.json) with Fabric/new-architecture as default, the old implicit ScrollResponder auto-scroll-to-focused-input behavior is not something this code opts into or can rely on, so the claim that the keyboard can cover these fields with no automatic scroll-into-view is technically accurate rather than a misreading. Crucially, this is not a hypothetical: the codebase's own convention proves the gap is real and inconsistent rather than intended. mobile/src/features/auth/sign-in-screen.tsx:39 explicitly wraps its BalenciaScreen in `<KeyboardAvoidingView behavior={Platform.select({ios:'padding'...})}>` specifically because it has TextInputs — establishing this as the house pattern for text-input screens — yet DataControlsScreen (and also cia-screen.tsx, cia-onboarding-screen.tsx) omit it entirely. The proposed fix (wrap the screen, or BalenciaScreen itself, in KeyboardAvoidingView / add explicit scroll-into-view on focus) is correct and minimal, mirroring the working precedent already in sign-in-screen.tsx. One mitigating factor worth noting for triage: the ScrollView still permits manual scrolling while the keyboard is shown (it isn't a hard blocker to completing the flow), which is why "high" rather than "critical" is defensible, but I found no basis to refute or downgrade the finding itself.

confirmed.title: Privacy Switch controls render below the 44px touch-target minimum
confirmed.detail: The three `<Switch>` toggles (lines 46-50, 54-58, 62-66) sit inside `toggleRow`/`visibilityContainer` views styled with `minHeight: TouchTarget` (44), but `alignItems: 'center'` only centers the fixed-intrinsic-size native Switch inside that taller row — it does not enlarge the Switch's own hit-testable bounds. The iOS UISwitch renders at its standard ~51x31pt size, so the actual tappable control is only ~31pt tall, under the AGENTS.md-mandated 44px minimum, and no `hitSlop` is applied to compensate.
confirmed.fix: Add `hitSlop={{ top: 7, bottom: 7 }}` (or equivalent) to each Switch, or wrap each Switch in a Pressable with a 44px minHeight that forwards the toggle, so the accessible/tappable region actually reaches 44px.
confirmed.verifyReason: Verified against actual file (mobile/src/features/trust/data-controls-screen.tsx:44-67) and RN internals shipped in node_modules. The three Switch elements sit in `toggleRow` (flexDirection:row, alignItems:'center', minHeight: TouchTarget=44) with no hitSlop, style, width, or height override on the Switch itself, so Yoga gives the Switch its native intrinsic size (iOS UISwitch ~51x31pt) — the parent's minHeight only makes the row taller and vertically centers the ~31pt-tall switch inside it; it does not enlarge the Switch's own hit-testable frame. Confirmed by reading RN 0.86's Fabric source (RCTSwitchComponentView.mm): the component subclasses RCTViewComponentView and inherits its stock -pointInside:/-hitTest: which insets self.bounds by hitTestEdgeInsets (set from the `hitSlop` prop) — RCTSwitchComponentView does not override this, so hitSlop is fully functional on Switch in this project's architecture (RN 0.86 defaults to new-arch/Fabric, confirmed via node_modules react-native package.json version). So (1) the claimed behavior is accurate — no hitSlop compensation exists and the tappable region is genuinely ~31pt, under the 44px minimum; (2) there is a concrete usability failure: a tap within the 44pt row but outside the ~31pt switch glyph (e.g., near the row's top/bottom edge) will not toggle the control, directly conflicting with mobile/AGENTS.md's explicit "44px minimum touch targets" rule — this is in-scope project policy, not a deferred BIOS-004 visual-parity concern; (3) the proposed fix (hitSlop={{top:7,bottom:7}} or an equivalent-sized wrapping Pressable) is correct and minimal — hitSlop is a valid, functional prop on RN's Switch (inherited from ViewProps/RCTViewComponentView) and the ~7pt top/bottom padding closes the ~13pt gap between the switch's ~31pt height and the 44px target, and the parent row (no clipsToBounds/overflow:hidden set) won't clip the expanded hit region. Severity: medium is appropriate — a real, HIG/AGENTS.md-violating touch-target defect, but the native switch is already a reasonably-sized 51x31 control so the shortfall is ~13pt, not a broken/unusable feature.

confirmed.title: Global 401 handler treats any endpoint's 401 as session-expiry and forces a refresh-token rotation
confirmed.detail: apiFetch() intercepts every non-skipAuth 401 response the same way: it calls refreshSession() (POST /auth/refresh, rotating the access+refresh token pair) and retries the original request once. This is correct for a stale access token, but the server also returns 401 for endpoint-specific business failures — e.g. DELETE /v1/users/me returns ApiError.unauthorized('Password is incorrect') for a wrong delete-account password (server/src/controllers/user.controller.ts:225), unrelated to token validity. Per session.ts's own comment, the server stores ONE refresh token per user, so every such spurious refresh() call rotates that single refresh token. A user who mistypes their delete-account password (mobile/src/features/trust/data-controls-screen.tsx handleDelete) therefore triggers an unrelated refresh-token rotation on every wrong attempt, which can silently invalidate a legitimate session on another signed-in device (the exact 'Multi-device caveat' session.ts:116-118 warns about), and the real error is re-thrown to the caller as SessionExpiredError instead of the intended 'wrong password' ApiError.
confirmed.fix: Scope the automatic refresh-and-retry-on-401 behavior to endpoints that actually depend on the access token's session validity (e.g. via a per-call flag, or by having the server return a distinct code such as UNAUTHORIZED vs INVALID_CREDENTIALS that the client can branch on), so a business-rule 401 from an endpoint like delete-account never triggers a refresh-token rotation or gets remapped to SessionExpiredError.
confirmed.verifyReason: Code fully corroborates the claim. client.ts:205 unconditionally triggers refreshSession() for any non-skipAuth 401, regardless of cause (verified: the `if (response.status === 401 && !skipAuth)` branch runs before body parsing, so it can't distinguish business-rule 401s from stale-token 401s). session.ts's refreshSession() unconditionally POSTs /auth/refresh with the stored refresh token whenever called — it doesn't know or care why the caller invoked it. Server-side, DELETE /v1/users/me (user.controller.ts:219-226) throws ApiError.unauthorized('Password is incorrect') — a 401 with code UNAUTHORIZED, textually indistinguishable from an expired-token 401 (auth.middleware.ts:46, same code/status). auth-session.controller.ts:106-181 confirms the server keeps exactly ONE hashed refresh_token per user and rewrites it on every successful /auth/refresh call — matching session.ts:116-118's own 'Multi-device caveat' comment. deleteMyAccount() (trust.ts:30-34) calls apiFetch with default skipAuth=false, so a wrong delete-password attempt does walk this exact path: spurious refresh → single stored refresh token rotated → retried DELETE still 401 → client throws SessionExpiredError instead of surfacing the real ApiError. (Note: the UI happens to still display 'Password is incorrect' because use-trust.ts:122 hardcodes that string for any ApiError with status 401 — SessionExpiredError extends ApiError so the check still matches — but this masks only the copy, not the underlying unwanted token rotation, which is the actual security-relevant defect.) I also confirmed the same overload pattern recurs at auth-session.controller.ts:404-406 (change-password's 'Current password is incorrect', also behind `authenticate`), so this is a systemic 401-overloading issue, not a one-off. The proposed fix (scope auto-refresh via a per-call flag, or have the server distinguish session-invalidity 401s from business-rule 401s via a distinct code) is directionally correct and minimal; a per-call `skipAutoRefresh` flag on ApiFetchOptions would be the smallest surgical fix. Severity 'high' is appropriate: this isn't visual/out-of-scope work, and it causes real unwanted session/refresh-token rotation with cross-device session-invalidation side effects, not just a cosmetic issue.

confirmed.title: Session-expiry purge (queryClient.clear + forced sign-in redirect) is only wired to the /auth/me path, not to any other query
confirmed.detail: handleAuthCleared() (which fires onAuthCleared -> queryClient.clear() in mobile/src/services/query/client.ts:33-35) and the SESSION_STATUS transition to 'expired' (which is the only thing that makes (tabs)/_layout.tsx redirect to sign-in, per its `status === 'expired'` check) are only dispatched from refreshUser() (line 76-83) and the boot() effect (line 106-114) — both of which call apiFetch('/auth/me'). None of the other data hooks that also call apiFetch and can receive the same SessionExpiredError (use-overview.ts, use-missions.ts, use-fitness.ts, use-life-areas.ts, use-cia-chat.ts via services/adapters/cia.ts) route that error back into the session machine. If the refresh token is invalidated (revoked, rotated by another device, expired) while the user is on any screen other than one that calls /auth/me, the UI stays in 'authenticated' status indefinitely: no forced sign-out, no queryClient.clear(), and the dead session stays in SecureStore. On a shared device this means the cross-account cache purge the design relies on (queryClient.clear() on sign-out/expiry) does not reliably fire the moment the session actually goes bad — only on explicit signOut() or a lucky /auth/me hit.
confirmed.fix: Add a global QueryCache-level (or apiFetch-level) hook that, on any SessionExpiredError, dispatches the same REFRESH_FAILURE/handleAuthCleared path used by refreshUser(), so session expiry detected from ANY endpoint forces the local session clear + cache purge + sign-in redirect, not just /auth/me.
confirmed.verifyReason: Verified against the actual code, not just the summary. `status === 'expired'` (the only thing (tabs)/_layout.tsx checks to force-redirect to sign-in, src/app/(tabs)/_layout.tsx:10) is set exclusively by dispatch({type:'REFRESH_FAILURE'}) in session-machine.ts, and a repo-wide grep confirms that dispatch — plus the onAuthCleared() call that triggers queryClient.clear() (services/query/client.ts:33-35) — fires from exactly two places: refreshUser() (session-provider.tsx:76-79) and the boot() effect (lines 109-112), both of which only call apiFetch('/auth/me'). Every other data hook inspected (use-overview.ts, use-missions.ts; use-cia-chat.ts goes through a separate sendCiaChat/classifyCiaError path that also never touches session state) calls apiFetch directly inside useQuery and never inspects SessionExpiredError to reset session state. Critically, the underlying refreshSession() in session.ts (invoked from apiFetch's reactive 401 handler on ANY endpoint, client.ts:205-223) explicitly handles the exact revoked/rotated-refresh-token scenario the finding describes (comment at session.ts:116-117: 'Multi-device caveat... A mismatch means another device rotated it. We transition to expired.') and calls clearSession() to wipe SecureStore — but never dispatches REFRESH_FAILURE or calls onAuthCleared/queryClient.clear(). So a session invalidated while the user is on any non-/auth/me screen leaves status stuck at 'authenticated', the cache uncleared, and the dead session absent from SecureStore but the UI unaware, until/unless a subsequent /auth/me call happens to fire. The proposed fix (route SessionExpiredError from any endpoint, e.g. via a QueryCache-level onError or a shared handler inside apiFetch/refreshSession, into the same REFRESH_FAILURE + handleAuthCleared path) is correct and minimal — it reuses existing plumbing rather than inventing new mechanism.

confirmed.title: Delete-account password is never cleared from component state after submit
confirmed.detail: handleDelete() reads `deletePassword` and calls runDelete({ password: deletePassword || undefined }) but never resets the `deletePassword` state afterward — not on success, and not on failure (e.g. wrong-password 401, where the component stays mounted and the user is expected to retry). The plaintext password remains sitting in the component's React state (and thus JS heap) for the lifetime of the mounted screen, contrary to the reviewed trust-lens expectation that a submitted password is not retained in memory afterward.
confirmed.fix: Call setDeletePassword('') (and consider setDeletePhrase('')) in a finally-style path immediately after runDelete() resolves, regardless of success/failure, so the plaintext password does not linger in memory past the submit attempt.
confirmed.verifyReason: Code behavior is confirmed exactly as described: handleDelete() (data-controls-screen.tsx:24-30) calls runDelete({ password: deletePassword || undefined }) and never calls setDeletePassword('') on either branch. Cross-checked use-trust.ts's useDeleteAccount: on a 401 (wrong password) it sets errorMessage and returns false without throwing further, so handleDelete's `if (success)` branch is skipped, no signOut/navigation occurs, and the screen stays mounted with deletePassword still holding the plaintext value in React state — matching the described wrong-password retry scenario exactly. The proposed fix (clear deletePassword, optionally deletePhrase, right after runDelete resolves regardless of outcome) is correct, minimal, and doesn't touch unrelated code. However, real-world severity doesn't reach 'medium': exploiting a password string sitting in JS heap requires local memory access on an already-compromised/jailbroken device — there's no network leak, no logging, no persistence beyond the mounted component's lifetime, and the same plaintext is already flowing through the bound (masked) TextInput regardless. No documented Balencia/mobile spec, canon, or AGENTS.md requirement was found mandating that submitted secrets be cleared from state on this screen — the finding's 'reviewed trust-lens expectation' appears to be the reviewer's own general security-hygiene standard rather than a project-committed requirement. This is a legitimate, correctly-scoped defense-in-depth hardening fix, appropriately labeled low severity rather than medium given the narrow, device-compromise-only exploitability.

confirmed.title: Me screen renders fabricated 'Level 0 / 0 XP / Streak 0' instead of an honest loading/null state
confirmed.detail: MetricTile values are computed as `${stats?.level ?? 0}` / `${stats?.xp.toLocaleString() ?? 0}` / `${stats?.streak ?? 0}` with no check on useGamification()'s query status (no pending/error branch exists in this component, unlike fitness-screen.tsx and missions-screen.tsx which gate on status). Combined with services/adapters/gamification.ts:21-29, which itself unconditionally coalesces `stats?.currentLevel ?? 1` / `stats?.totalXP ?? 0` / `stats?.currentStreak ?? 0` with no provenance/null wrapper (contrast with life-areas.ts and fitness.ts, which correctly wrap in Metric<T> with fromNullable/nullMetric for an honest '—' null state), this means every load — even before the query resolves — displays literal invented numbers ('Level 0', '0 XP', 'Streak 0') as if they were real user data, violating the honesty invariant that governs every other screen touched in this batch.
confirmed.fix: Gate me-screen.tsx on the query's status (pending/error) the same way fitness-screen.tsx and missions-screen.tsx do, and have services/adapters/gamification.ts return a null/HonestNullState-compatible shape (or Metric<T> with provenance) instead of defaulting missing stats to 0/1, so 'no data yet' is never rendered as a real number.
confirmed.verifyReason: Verified against actual code. me-screen.tsx:12 calls `const { data: stats } = useGamification()` with no destructure/check of `status`, unlike fitness-screen.tsx and missions-screen.tsx (both read `status`, `refetch` and branch on `status === 'pending'` → SkeletonState, `status === 'error' || !data` → ErrorState, and empty-data → HonestNullState before rendering any real values). me-screen.tsx:20-21 renders `${stats?.level ?? 0}`, `${stats?.xp.toLocaleString() ?? 0}`, `${stats?.streak ?? 0}` unconditionally, so on first mount (query pending) or on fetch failure, `stats` is `undefined` and the screen prints literal 'Level 0', '0 XP', 'Streak 0' as if it were real user data — with no skeleton, error, or honest-null indicator. This is exactly the pending/error window the finding describes, and it's provably distinguishable from real data: services/adapters/gamification.ts:21 already defaults a genuinely-missing-but-present `stats` object's level to `1` (`stats?.currentLevel ?? 1`), so any real StatsVM after the query resolves never naturally renders 'Level 0' — meaning 'Level 0' can only appear in the undefined/loading/error case, confirming it's a fabricated placeholder, not a legitimate default. Cross-checked services/adapters/fitness.ts, which wraps ambiguous/missing values in `Metric<T>`/`nullMetric(...)` for exactly this honesty reason, confirming the codebase's own established convention that this finding says gamification.ts violates. Git history confirms me-screen.tsx was explicitly touched in the same BIOS-002 batch commit (7529e8b, 'Me on live stats') alongside Today/Missions/LifeAreas/Fitness, which the same commit message says got Skeleton/Error/HonestNull states and 'fabrications deleted' — so this is not out-of-batch-scope drift, it's an inconsistency within the very batch that established the honesty pattern. No waiver for this gap was found in plans/batches/BIOS-002-ios-simulator-contracts/BATCH.md or scope-map.json (scope-map.json:391 lists me.tsx's level/streak metrics as in-scope with no waiver annotation). The proposed fix (gate on query status like the sibling screens, and have the adapter emit a Metric/nullable-aware shape instead of silently defaulting) is correct and minimal, mirroring existing sibling-screen and sibling-adapter patterns already in the codebase.
